But we're not told why.

We might speculate why -- "Record companies have decided to put their money into repackaging vintage recordings rather than into developing new talent and new recordings".

However, we are told that we was signed to Columbia and that Columbia still has some roster of active jazz musicians. Why isn't Marsalis, one of the biggest brand names in active jazz musicians, one of those artists? We don't know.

choices.text: What is a factor that contributed to the shift by record companies toward reissuing vintage jazz recordings?
choices.explanation:
In the 4th paragraph, we're told how Marsalis' great emphasis on past masters ultimately influenced record companies' decision to reissue vintage jazz recordings.

He told young musicians to pay attention to the music's traditions. He put emphasis on the past masters. And even though he meant "let's take traditional elements and recombine them or reinvent them to push the genre forward", *record executives came away with a different message*.

So a factor that contributed to the shift toward reissuing vintage jazz recordings was the way Marsalis strongly promoted the past masters to younger audiences.

passages.title: Inferential Thoughts
passages.text:
Common sense suggests that we know our own thoughts directly, but that we infer the thoughts of other people. The former process is noninferential and infallible, while the latter is based on others’ behavior and can always be wrong. But this assumption is challenged by experiments in psychology demonstrating that in certain circumstances young children tend to misdescribe their own thoughts regarding simple phenomena while nonetheless correctly describing those phenomena. It seems that these children have the same thoughts that adults have regarding the phenomena but are much less capable of identifying these thoughts. Some psychologists argue that this indicates that one’s awareness of one’s own thoughts is every bit as inferential as one’s awareness of another person’s thoughts. According to their interpretation of the experiments, thoughts are unobservable entities that, among other things, help to explain why we act as we do. It follows from this that we are wrong to think of ourselves as having noninferential and infallible access to our own thoughts.

Recognizing an obligation to explain why we cling so tenaciously to an illusory belief in noninferential and infallible knowledge of our own thoughts, these psychologists suggest that this illusion is analogous to what happens to us when we become experts in a particular area. Greater expertise appears to change not only our knowledge of the area as a whole, but our very perception of entities in that area. It appears to us that we become able to see and to grasp these entities and their relations directly, whereas before we could only make inferences about them. For instance, chess experts claim the ability to see without calculation whether a position is weak or strong. From a psychological perspective, we become so expert in making incredibly fast introspective inferences about our thinking that we fail to notice that we are making them. This failure leads naturally to the supposition that there is no way for us to be wrong in our identification of what we ourselves think because we believe we are perceiving it directly.

In claiming that we have only inferential access to our thoughts, the psychologists come perilously close to claiming that we base our inferences about what we ourselves are thinking solely on observations of our own external behavior. But, in fact, their arguments do not commit them to this claim; the psychologists suggest that we are somehow able to base our inferences about what we are thinking on internal cognitive activity that is not itself thought—e.g., fleeting and instantaneous sensations and emotions. The frequent occurrence of such internal activities explains why we develop the capacity to make quick and reliable inferences. Their internality makes it impossible for anyone else to make an inference based on them that contradicts our own. Thus, they are crucial in creating the illusion of noninferentiality and infallibility.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Whether our knowledge of our own thoughts is direct and infallible, or actually inferential and potentially fallible

**Framework**

Challenge Position

**Main Point**

The passage challenges the common belief that we have direct, infallible access to our own thoughts and suggests, based on psychological experiments, that our knowledge of our own thoughts is actually inferential—much like how we infer the thoughts of others. *The Most Valuable Sentence is at the end of the first paragraph: "It follows from this that we are wrong to think of ourselves as having noninferential and infallible access to our own thoughts."*

**P1: Challenging Common Sense about Self-Knowledge**

Common sense says we know our own thoughts directly and with certainty, but experiments show young children can misdescribe their own thoughts, even when they get the actual facts right. Psychologists use this to argue that our self-knowledge is actually inferential, just like when we guess what others are thinking.

**P2: Explaining Why We Think We're Infallible**

These psychologists try to explain why we're so convinced we know our thoughts directly. They compare it to gaining expertise—like chess experts who "just see" a good move. We become so skilled at quickly and unconsciously figuring out what we're thinking that it feels like direct perception, even though it's not.

**P3: Refining the Position—What Are We Inferring From?**

The psychologists clarify that, even if our self-knowledge is inferential, we aren't just looking at our own external behavior. Instead, we draw on our internal experiences—like fleeting emotions or sensations—to make these inferences. Because no one else can observe these internal cues, our mistaken sense of infallibility is reinforced.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The central topic of this passage was the question of whether or not we know our thoughts perfectly and directly, or whether we infer what we're thinking and could potentially be wrong about it.

The author is mainly presenting the ideas of psychologists. She occasionally makes her voice known by guiding the conversation, but for the most part we don't get an author evaluation like "These ideas are right / wrong".

We'd probably use an *Answer a Question* framework, since the central topic is trying to solve the causal mystery of whether we truly have infallible, direct access to our thoughts.

The author seems to be entertaining the somewhat radical idea that we **don't** have infallible, direct access.

This alternative story is that we make inferences about what we're thinking. It *feels* direct and infallible because we're such experts at inferring our own thoughts that we do it instantly. Since we do it so instantly, we fail to notice we're even doing it.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Look for a sentence that somewhat sympathetically platforms the ideas of these psychologists: "While we assume we have direct, infallible access to our own thoughts, some psychologists suggest that we might just be really good at inferring our own thoughts."

choices.text: Only experts within a given domain have noninferential and infallible access to their own thoughts; other people must infer their own thoughts as they do others' thoughts.
choices.explanation:
The passage was never arguing that experts have noninferential and infallible access to their own thoughts, let alone that **only** they do.

Our author is considering these new ideas and doesn't have any clear position on them yet, so it's also too strong to say that "other people **must** infer their own thoughts".

Experts are brought up to make an analogy: just as an expert chess player feels like they have direct knowledge of the pieces on a chess board, a normal human is an expert at their own thinking so they feel like they have direct knowledge of it.

choices.text: In opposition to the common belief that thoughts are directly perceived, some psychologists argue that people infer what their own thoughts are.
choices.explanation:
The main clause is that "some psychologists argue that people infer what their own thoughts are".

That fits the central topic and noncommittal vibe of the author. The warm-up clause here establishes the *Old* assumption that we directly perceive our own thoughts. The main clause summarizes this *New* idea that maybe we infer our own thoughts.

choices.text: In response to the common belief that thoughts are directly perceived, some psychologists claim that this belief is an illusion resulting from our inability to make quick and reliable inferences.
choices.explanation: This is super close, but the psychologists would say "this belief is an illusion resulting from our **ability** to make quick and reliable inferences about our own thinking".

choices.text: Some psychologists have recently attributed children's failure to give an accurate description of their own thoughts to their lack of expertise.
choices.explanation:
The central topic of this passage was **not** children's failure to give an accurate description of their own thoughts.

So we can stop reading there. That experiment was just a launchpad for this broader inquiry about whether we know our thoughts directly or indirectly.

choices.text: Some psychologists hold that people are able to make inferences about what they are thinking that are based solely on observing their own external behavior.
choices.explanation: The beginning of the final paragraph says that the psychologists come *perilously close* to saying this, but do not actually hold these beliefs: "their arguments **do not** commit them to this claim".

questions.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question the psychologists' interpretation of the experiments with children (fourth and fifth sentences of the first paragraph)?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Let's remind ourselves what the psychologists' interpretation was.

*Curious Fact ...* why is it that young children will misdescribe their own thoughts regarding simple phenomena, even though they can correctly describe those phenomena?

*Psychologists' Interpretation ...* this indicates that our awareness of our own thoughts is every bit as inferential as our awareness of someone else's thoughts, and these kids are making bad inferences about what they were thinking.

We know there are always to two ways to Weaken when we're analyzing someone's causal hypothesis for a curious fact:
1. suggest an *Alternate Explanation* (more common)
2. say something that hurts the *Plausibility* of the author's explanation

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's primarily look for an answer that offers a different explanation for why the kids misdescribed their own thoughts, or maybe an answer that hurts the plausibility that the kids were making bad inferences about what their thoughts were.

choices.text: Some children who took part in the experiments were no less capable than some adults at identifying their own thoughts.
choices.explanation:
This has nothing to do with offering an Alternate Explanation for why kids tend to misdecribe their own thoughts, and it does nothing to debunk the plausibility of the story that "these kids were misdescribing thoughts because they were less adept at inferring what their thoughts are". This answer isn't even about the kids we're focused on, the ones who were messing up identifying their own thoughts.

The fact that *some* kids **were** adept and didn't misdescribe their thoughts changes nothing. We never thought that **all** kids were messing up. We just knew most of them were. They **tended** to misdescribe their own thoughts.

p.s. Answers with the puny strength of "some / sometimes / can / may" are usually not right on Strengthen or Weaken, in both LR and RC.

choices.text: Experiments with older children found that they were as accurate as adults in identifying their thoughts.
choices.explanation:
Since this deals with older children, whereas the Curious Fact is about the young children in the study, this isn't going to be an *Alternate Explanation* for why the young kids tended to misdescribe their thoughts.

Does it hurt the plausibility of the author's story, if we say that older children are as good as adults at identifying their thoughts?

No, they're older children! Their brains have apparently developed enough to make quick, solid, reliable inferences about their thinking (to use the psychologists' wording).

Their ability to *not* make errors doesn't affect the author's explanation for why younger kids *did* make errors.

choices.text: The limited language skills possessed by young children make it difficult for them to accurately communicate their thoughts.
choices.explanation:
This provides an *Alternate Explanation* for the curious fact, which is arguably the biggest tendency among Weaken questions.

This let's us question the psychologists' interpretation by saying, "Hmm, *maybe* kids were misdescribing their thoughts because none of us really know our thoughts and we're all just inferring potentially fallible guesses about what our thoughts are and kids just aren't good enough at that inferential skill to make accurate guesses yet .... or ... *maybe* kids misdescribed their thoughts because their limited language skills made it hard for them to accurately describe their thoughts."

choices.text: Most young children cannot be expected to know the difference between direct and indirect access to one's thoughts.
choices.explanation:
The author doesn't care, nor do we, whether kids know the difference between direct and indirect access to thoughts. That has nothing to do with offering an Alternate Explanation for why the young kids misdescribed their thoughts.

And it has nothing to do with hurting the plausibility of the psychologists' explanation.

choices.text: The psychologists who conducted the experiments with children were concerned with psychological issues other than the nature of people's access to their own thoughts.
choices.explanation:
It doesn't matter whether the psychologists *intended* to discover X or not. In science, we often make discoveries accidentally, tangentially to what we went there to study.

Viagra, the erectile dysfunction medication, was originally supposed to be a heart medication. The clinical researchers conducting the Viagra trials were concerned with its effects on the heart, but once they got inescapable data about the surprising "side effect" of this drug, they realized that their chemical formula was causing these erectile side effects.

So we can't make their interpretation look bad by saying, "They weren't concerned with discovering something like this when they embarked on this research".

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, the author is most likely to believe which one of the following about the view that "we base our inferences about what we ourselves are thinking solely on observations of our own external behavior" (first sentence of third paragraph)?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
At the beginning of the final paragraph, the author tells us that these psychologists come ****perilously**** close to claiming this view, but, in fact, their arguments do not commit them to that claim.

What does it mean to come ****perilously**** close to claiming a certain view?

A synonym for "perilously close" would be "dangerously close". Why would it be dangerous to hold the view that "we base our inferences about what we ourselves are thinking solely on observations of our own external behavior"?

In the context of this passage, the author is sort of saying, "These psychologists have got my attention. I'm sympathetic to their interpretation. I'm listening. They came ****dangerously close**** to losing me, though. If they had said we determine what we're thinking solely by observing our external behavior, I'd be out. That's a super dumb thing to say."

Why is it dumb?

Well, are you having thoughts right now? Of course you are. Are you deciding what you're thinking purely by observing your own external behavior?

Of course not. If we based inferences about what we're thinking solely on observations of our own external behavior, then closing our eyes would shut off our thoughts. After all, if we can't observe our external behavior, we can't infer our thoughts, according to this view.

The author, and all of us with common sense, know that thinking is taking place internally. You'd never convince us that we figure out our thoughts by observing our external behavior, because our bodies could be motionless even while our mind is racing.

So the author was saying to us readers, "you might be worried that the psychologists are essentially selling us on this absurd takeaway, but don't worry, they aren't saying anything that crazy."

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Look for something like it is an implausible view that the psychologists have *not* committed themselves to.

choices.text: It constitutes a denial of the possibility of scientifically studying thinking processes.
choices.explanation:
This notion of "it denies the possibility of scientifically studying thinking" isn't reinforced by any nearby wording. And it's even counterintuitive. After all, if thinking were solely based on observations of *external* behavior, it would actually be way easier to study someone's thinking.

The scientist would have access to the same external behavior observations that the thinker can observe. In reality, the fact that thinking is coming from some internal behavior is what makes it much harder (much less possible) to scientifically study.

choices.text: It has often been misunderstood by psychologists.
choices.explanation:
We have no support for the idea that these or any other psychologists have ever held this view. Our author is communicating to us that the psychologists in this passage ****do not**** hold this view.

And the author isn't saying, "Psychologists misunderstand this view". She's more saying, "Phew -- these psychologists have enough common sense to avoid subscribing to this view."

choices.text: It was the prevailing view until undermined by recent psychology experiments.
choices.explanation:
The prevailing view was not that we infer our thinking based solely on ****external**** observations.

It was (from the 1st sentence of the passage) that *we know our thoughts directly,* which means
1. we're ****not inferring**** them at all
2. they're ****internal**** to our mind

choices.text: It seems to contradict common sense but is basically sound.
choices.explanation: The author is not saying this view is basically sound. The author is saying that it does contradict common sense, and so thankfully the psychologists are not committing to this deeply implausible view.

choices.text: It is not considered to be an intellectually defensible position.
choices.explanation:
This answer certainly takes us aback, because of how strong it is and how there isn't any nearby synonym for "intellectually indefensible".

But it is supported by the language of, "they came ****dangerously**** close to saying something like this view, but lucky for them their arguments do not commit them to this claim".

However, we also need to use some of our own common sense to understand the intended contextual meaning. Why would it be dangerous for them to have this view? Because this view, common sense tells us, has *got* to be wrong! There's no way we infer our thinking solely by observing the external behavior of our bodies.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is most closely analogous to the explanation in the passage of how persons fail to notice that they are making inferences about their thoughts?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The explanation at the end of the 2nd paragraph is saying that, "the reason we don't notice that we're actually *inferring* our thoughts (rather than directly perceiving them) is because ... **we become so expert in making incredibly fast inferences**."

So we need an answer that says, "because were such experts at doing X, because we do it so instantly / automatically, we don't notice that we're doing X".

choices.text: An anthropologist cannot describe his own culture accurately because he has become too familiar with its workings and therefore takes them for granted.
choices.explanation:
This provides us our best available match.

CAUSE EFFECT

This language doesn't all line up perfectly, but there's an overall similarity of "you know yourself so well that you don't realize certain things about yourself (like that you're making inferences about your thinking)" just like "you know your country's culture so well that you don't realize certain things about it".

choices.text: Science is limited with regard to studying the human mind because science necessarily depends on human reasoning.
choices.explanation:
It's hard to match up either half of this.

CAUSE EFFECT

so expert in making we fail to notice
inferences about X we're doing X

X depends on X is limited when
human reasoning it comes to humans

We could say that we're limited in our ability to notice we're making inferences about our own thinking, but it's not because that process depends on human reasoning.

After all, making inferences about other people's behavior is something we *do* notice ourselves doing, even though that also relies on human reasoning.

choices.text: As they develop, children become increasingly comfortable with formal abstraction and therefore become vulnerable to failures to learn from concrete experiences.
choices.explanation:
It's hard to match up either half of this.

CAUSE EFFECT

so expert in making we fail to notice
inferences about X we're doing X

become increasingly harder to learn

choices.text: Judges are barred from trying cases involving their family members because of a potential conflict of interest.
choices.explanation:
It's hard to match up either half of this.

CAUSE EFFECT

so expert in making we fail to notice
inferences about X we're doing X

potential conflict barred from

choices.text: A ship's commander must delegate certain duties and decisions to other officers on her ship because she is too busy to attend to those duties and decisions.
choices.explanation:
It's hard to match up either half of this.

CAUSE EFFECT

so expert in making we fail to notice

questions.prompt: According to the passage, one's gaining greater expertise in a field appears to result in

explanationBlocks.heading: Support Window
explanationBlocks.body:
Where does the passage discuss "gaining greater expertise in a field"? It's in the middle of the 2nd paragraph.

What does gaining expertise appear to result in?

*****it appears***** *to us that we become able to see and to grasp these entities and their relations directly, whereas before we could only make inferences about them.*

So we just want to look for the answer choice that sounds the most like that sentence. We can try putting this sentence into our own words first, to try to better digest its meaning (since correct answers usually use *different wording* to create a similar meaning).

The sentence is saying that "we used to feel like we saw things indirectly (like an amateur chess player would directly notice that a queen was under threat from the opponent's bishop and rook, and then think, *'Yikes, this is a weak position for my queen'*) but now we can perceive them directly (the expert chess player just looks at the board and *directly* sees '*Weak position')."*

choices.text: an altered way of expressing one's judgments about issues in that field
choices.tag: Out of Window: issues in that field
choices.explanation:
Nowhere in our support window does it talk about ****expressing**** one's judgments about ****issues**** in the field.

Our answer needs to match this text:
*it appears* *to us that we become able to see and to grasp these entities and their relations directly, whereas before we could only make inferences about them.*

choices.text: a more detail-oriented approach to questions in that field
choices.explanation:
Nowhere in our support window does it talk about a more detail-oriented approach. This is probably closer to the opposite of what we want, because the text is saying that the expert starts to holistically see the whole thing immediately (whereas detail-oriented approach sounds more like collecting individual facts before reaching a judgment).

Our answer needs to match this text:
*it appears* *to us that we become able to see and to grasp these entities and their relations directly, whereas before we could only make inferences about them.*

choices.text: an increased tendency to ignore one's own errors in judgment within that field
choices.tag: Out of Window: ignore own errors
choices.explanation:
Nowhere in our support window does it talk about ****ignoring your errors.****

Our answer needs to match this text:
*it appears* *to us that we become able to see and to grasp these entities and their relations directly, whereas before we could only make inferences about them.*

choices.text: a substantively different way of understanding relations within that field
choices.explanation:
Our answer needs to match this text:

*it appears* *to us that we become able to see and to grasp these entities and their* *****relations***** *directly, whereas before we could only make inferences about them.*

This answer seems accurate.
*before, we could only* *****make inferences***** *about entities and relations*
*now, we have become able to* *****see and grasp***** *these relations directly.*

Going from indirect inferential understanding of relations to directly grasping them seems to qualify as a substantively different way of understanding.

choices.text: a reduced reliance on sensations and emotions when inferring one's thoughts regarding that field
choices.tag: Out of Window: sensations / emotions / Contradicted: inferring
choices.explanation:
Our answer needs to match this text:

*it appears* *to us that we become able to see and to grasp these entities and their relations directly, whereas before we could only make inferences about them.*

Nothing in there talks about sensations or emotions, and the text specifically tells us that we ****no longer**** make inferences, so the part of this answer that says we're *inferring our thoughts* would be contradicted.

questions.prompt: According to the psychologists cited in the passage, the illusion of direct knowledge of our own thoughts arises from the fact that

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Where does the passage get into why psychologists think we have the illusion of direct knowledge about our own thoughts?

The 2nd paragraph is saying that psychologists realize they need to explain why we cling so tenaciously to the "illusory belief in noninferential (direct) knowledge of our own thoughts".

They say that the illusion is analogous to what happens when you become an expert.
- you feel like you can see and grasp things directly
- but really, you have just become so expert in making incredibly fast introspective inferences about our thinking that we fail to notice we are making them.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Look for something like, "it arises from the change in perception that results of becoming an expert" or "it arises from our expertise in making incredibly fast introspective inferences about our thinking".

choices.text: we ignore the feedback that we receive regarding the inaccuracy of the inferences we make about our thought processes
choices.tag: Not in Support Window: ignore feedback
choices.explanation: Nothing in the 2nd paragraph is saying that we *ignore* feedback telling us that the inferences we made about our thinking were actually inaccurate.

choices.text: knowledge of our own thoughts is usually unmediated due to our expertise, and we simply overlook instances where this is not the case
choices.explanation:
"Unmediated" = direct
Going through a mediator is indirect.

Would these psychologists say that knowledge of our own thoughts is usually ****direct****? No, they're saying it's indirect; we're just so expert at inferring our thoughts indirectly that we make them so fast it feels like direct perception of them.

choices.text: we are unaware of the inferential processes that allow us to become aware of our thoughts
choices.explanation:
Yes, this matches well with one of the two sentences in our Support Window:

*We become so expert in making incredibly fast introspective inferences about our thinking that we fail to notice that we are making [inferences about our thinking].*

The illusion that we have direct access to our thoughts arises from the fact that we don't realize we've actually made a lightning fast inference about our thinking, so it feels like we are just directly perceiving the thought.

choices.text: our inferences regarding our own thoughts are generally extremely accurate, as are our perceptions of the world
choices.explanation:
Nothing in the 2nd paragraph is saying our perceptions of the world are generally extremely accurate.

It doesn't actually say discuss the *accuracy* of our inferences about our own thoughts, either, but at least that's an area where presumably we are usually correct.

choices.text: our inferences regarding our own thoughts are sometimes clouded and uncertain, as are our perceptions of the world
choices.tag: Not in Support Window: ignore feedback
choices.explanation: Nothing in the 2nd paragraph is saying that we have an illusion of direct knowledge of thoughts because our inferences are sometimes "clouded and uncertain". That doesn't even make logical sense. Why would cloudy, uncertain inferences make us think we had pure, clear, direct access?

questions.prompt: It can most reasonably be inferred that the choice of children as the subjects of the psychology experiments discussed in the passage was advantageous to the experimenters for which one of the following reasons?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
So we're looking for why it was *advantageous* (i.e. helpful) for experimenters to choose children as the subjects of the psychology experiments.

If we re-read the snippet in the first paragraph that discusses the children in the experiments, this is a recap of ****what**** we know:

- in certain circumstances young children tend to misdescribe their own thoughts regarding simple phenomena while still being correct about the phenomena

- seems like the kids have the same thoughts about the phenomena as the adults, but *the kids are less capable of identifying these thoughts.*

Okay! So we've isolated the difference of children vs. adults. They both describe the phenomena in comparable ways, but the children are much less capable of identifying their thoughts (they misdescribe them).

So ****why**** is that *advantageous* to the experimenters? Well the goal of these experimenters is to show us that we don't know our own thoughts as well as we think we do, so the ****mismatch**** that a kid can provide between "they know the phenomena, but they don't know their own thoughts" helps to demonstrate how our thoughts about our own thinking is not infallible. If the kids are misdescribing their own thoughts, then they're helping the experimenters to show that we might be fallible about our understanding of our own thoughts.

So let's look for an answer that's like, "kids are a good choice, because they mess up describing their own thoughts, and so they help demonstrate that we actually can be fallible about our own thoughts'.

choices.text: Experiments involving children are more likely to give interesting results because children are more creative than adults.
choices.explanation: The distinction we're being tested on is that children are *more likely to be incapable of describing their own thoughts*.

choices.text: Adults are more likely than children to give inaccurate reports of their thought processes.
choices.explanation: This is the correct idea, but assigned to the wrong parties. The children are more likely to give inaccurate reports of their thought processes.

choices.text: Since adults are infallible in their access to their own thoughts, only the thought processes of children shed light on the nature of inference.
choices.explanation:
The whole point of this passage is that experimenters are suggesting it's possible that we're ****all**** fallible when it comes to our own thoughts, so we can't sign off on saying "adults are infallible in their access to their own thoughts".

From the experimenters' point of view, we're all fallible, but children will be an easier way to demonstrate that.

choices.text: Mental processes are sometimes easier to study in children because children are more likely than adults to make certain cognitive errors.
choices.explanation:
The distinction we're being tested on is that "children are much less capable (than adults) of identifying the thoughts they have regarding simple phenomena".

In certain circumstances, young children "tend to misdescribe their own thoughts". That qualifies as a *cognitive error*.

choices.text: Children are less experienced than adults in inferring the thoughts of others from observations of their behavior.
choices.explanation:
In the final paragraph, the author makes clear that these psychologists are ****not**** saying the crazy claim that we infer our own thoughts by observing our own behavior (they came *perilously close* to saying that bunk, but no).

The explanation favored by these psychologists is that we infer our thoughts from internal phenomena. So this answer could have probably worked if it said that "kids are less experienced at inferring their own thoughts from their own internal cognitive activity".

passages.title: Dowsing
passages.text:
*This passage is based on an article written in 1995.*

Dowsing is the practice of detecting resources or objects beneath the ground by passing handheld, inert tools such as forked sticks, pendulums, or metal rods over a terrain. For example, dowsers typically determine prospective water-well drilling locations by walking with a horizontally held forked tree branch until it becomes vertical, claiming the branch is pulled to this position. The distance to the water from the surface and the potential well’s flow rate are then determined by holding the branch horizontally again and either walking in place or backwards while the branch is pulled vertical again. The number of paces indicates the distance to the water, and the strength of the pull felt by the dowser correlates with the potential well’s flow rate.

Those skeptical of dowsing’s efficacy point to the crudeness of its methods as a self-evident reason to question it. They assert that dowsers’ use of inert tools indicates that the dowsers themselves actually make subconscious determinations concerning the likely location of groundwater using clues derived from surface conditions; the tools’ movements merely reflect the dowsers’ subconscious thoughts. Further, skeptics say, numerous studies show that while a few dowsers have demonstrated considerable and consistent success, the success rate for dowsers generally is notably inconsistent. Finally, skeptics note, dowsing to locate groundwater is largely confined to areas where groundwater is expected to be ubiquitous, making it statistically unlikely that a dowsed well will be completely dry.

Proponents of dowsing point out that it involves a number of distinct techniques and contend that each of these techniques should be evaluated separately. They also note that numerous dowsing studies have been influenced by a lack of care in selecting the study population; dowsers are largely self-proclaimed and self-certified, and verifiably successful dowsers are not well represented in the typical study. Proponents claim that successful dowsers may be sensitive to minute changes in Earth’s electromagnetic field associated with variations in subsurface conditions. They also claim that these dowsers have higher success rates than geologists and hydrologists who use scientific tools such as electromagnetic sensors or seismic readings to locate groundwater.

The last two claims were corroborated during a recent and extensive study that utilized teams of the most successful dowsers, geologists, and hydrologists to locate reliable water supplies in various arid countries. Efforts were concentrated on finding groundwater in narrow, tilted fracture zones in bedrock underlying surface sediments. The teams were unfamiliar with the areas targeted, and they agreed that no surface clues existed that could assist in pinpointing the locations of fracture zones. The dowsers consistently made significantly more accurate predictions regarding drill sites, and on request even located a dry fracture zone, suggesting that dowsers can detect variations in subsurface conditions.

summaries.standard:
**Topic**

The effectiveness and legitimacy of dowsing (using handheld tools to locate underground water) as compared to scientific methods.

**Framework**

*Present Debate*

**Main Point**

There is ongoing debate about whether dowsing is a valid technique for locating groundwater; while skeptics offer several criticisms and point to evidence against its effectiveness, recent studies have shown that experienced dowsers sometimes outperform scientific experts in locating water in challenging conditions. (The most valuable summary sentence appears at the end of the last paragraph: "The dowsers consistently made significantly more accurate predictions regarding drill sites, and on request even located a dry fracture zone, suggesting that dowsers can detect variations in subsurface conditions.")

**P1: What is Dowsing?**

Dowsing is explained as a method where people use handheld items, like a forked stick, to "find" underground water. The dowser believes the tool moves in response to water sources, and the number of movements supposedly indicates both well depth and flow rate.

**P2: Skeptics' Criticisms**

Skeptics dismiss dowsing as too crude to be effective. They argue that dowsers are just unconsciously using clues from the surface, and the tool's movements merely reflect subconscious judgments. To further discredit dowsing, skeptics note that any successes are inconsistent and tend to occur in areas where finding groundwater by chance is likely.

**P3: Proponents' Defense**

Supporters of dowsing argue that there are many techniques and not all have been studied equally. They say studies are flawed because they mostly use self-declared dowsers, not verifiably successful ones. Proponents suggest that skilled dowsers might actually sense changes in the Earth's electromagnetic field, and they even claim these dowsers outperform scientists using traditional scientific methods.

**P4: Evidence from a Recent Study**

A recent large-scale study compared the best dowsers to geologists and hydrologists in hard-to-assess areas. When none of the experts could rely on visible surface clues, the dowsers consistently made the best predictions, even successfully locating where water wouldn't be found—implying that there could be something real to their abilities.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes the primary purpose of the second paragraph?

choices.text: to add detail to the description presented in the first paragraph
to offer two perspectives that are synthesized into a new perspective presented in the final paragraph
to present arguments against which the third paragraph presents counterarguments
to explore in detail the ramifications of one claim made in the first paragraph
to clarify the issues on both sides in a dispute that the third paragraph attempts to resolve

questions.prompt: According to the passage, dowsing's skeptics acknowledge which one of the following?

choices.text: A few dowsers have shown considerable and consistent success.
Dowsing techniques are generally rejected by scientists.
Successful dowsers are not well represented in the typical study of dowsing's efficacy.
Successful dowsers may be sensitive to minute changes in Earth's electromagnetic field.

questions.prompt: The reasoning in which one of the following is most analogous to an argument explicitly attributed to dowsing's skeptics in the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The question stem ominously says that we're going match up our answer with **an** argument made by a skeptic.

Does that mean that there are multiple arguments made by skeptics? Yeesh. Okay, let's see which one(s) we can find.

The 2nd paragraph seems to have multiple arguments from skeptics:

1. The methods are so crude, how could it possibly be real? (how could holding a stick possibly help someone locate groundwater)

2. The "tools" do nothing besides reflect thoughts the user is having.

3. The success rate is very inconsistent (some people are very successful using this method; others aren't)

4. The technique is mainly used in areas where no matter where you decide to look, you're going to find some groundwater.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
That's a frustratingly wide net. We'll have to stay flexible as we read the answers and see if we can match any of these skeptical arguments:

"X doesn't really help you do Y, after all ..."
- X is too crude a method to do Y
- The tool used for X can't possibly do anything but reveal the user's thoughts
- the success rate of people using X to do Y is highly variable
- X is mainly used in an area where you're bound to achieve Y no matter what

choices.text: Some weather analysts claim that no one can forecast the weather a week ahead with better than 40 percent accuracy, but some computer models have been known to perform with more accuracy than that.
choices.explanation:
It's hard to even call this answer choice *reasoning*. There isn't a conclusion/premise here, just two contrasting thoughts.

The idea of *computers* doing better than what some people think any *person* can do doesn't match up with any of the skeptics' arguments against dowsing.

choices.text: Some people claim to have seen ghosts, but very few of these people can adduce even the smallest piece of credible evidence to support their claims.
choices.explanation:
It looks like all the answers are set up in this non-reasoning format. We're apparently supposed to assume in each case that the 2nd claim, the "but" claim, is supporting an implied conclusion that "We are skeptical of the 1st claim".

This "argument" is saying, "We should be skeptical that ghosts exist, because very few people who say they do exist can show even the smallest piece of credible evidence".

Did the skeptics say, "We should be skeptical that dowsing is effective, because very few dowsers can show even the smallest piece of credible evidence"?

No. It was "crude tools / inconsistent success rate / done in areas that unfairly favor success". We need one of those.

choices.text: Some musicians perform so well that their performances have been said to express a pure, innate talent, but such performances are in fact due to years of very intense practice.
choices.explanation:
This "argument" is saying, "We should be skeptical that certain awesome musicians are that way because of a pure, innate talent, because in reality they've just practiced a lot."

Did the skeptics say, "We should be skeptical that dowsing is effective, because in reality dowsers have just practiced a lot"?

No. It was "crude tools / inconsistent success rate / done in areas that unfairly favor success". We need one of those.

choices.text: Some people claim to be able to sense where the area's good fishing spots are, but the lakes in the area are so loaded with fish it would be difficult not to pick a good spot.
choices.explanation:
This "argument" is saying, "We should be skeptical when people claim they have the ability to sense good fishing spots, because this lake is so loaded with fish that any spot you pick is going to have fish."

Did the skeptics say, "We should be skeptical that dowsing is effective, because the area where people dowse is so loaded with groundwater that any spot you pick is going to have groundwater"?

Yes! That's the last sentence of the 2nd paragraph.

"Areas where groundwater is expected to be ubiquitous" = *lakes are so loaded with fish*

"it's statistically unlikely that a dowsed well will be completely dry" = *it would be difficult not to pick a good spot*

choices.text: Some people have memories of participating in historical events in which they did not actually participate, but this does not prove that they have been reincarnated.
choices.explanation:
This drifts even farther from any skeptical "argument". No one here is claiming anything that a skeptic could rebut.

The author is just telling us that when someone has a memory of participating in a historical event, that doesn't prove they have been reincarnated.

She doesn't offer any reason for that skepticism, so there's nothing here to even try to match up with the rationale of dowsing skeptics..

questions.prompt: The author of the passage would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the results of the groundwater-locating study discussed in the final paragraph?

The results leave open the possibility that dowsers can sense minute changes in Earth's electromagnetic field.
The results prove conclusively that dowsing is the most dependable technique for finding water in arid countries.
The results demonstrate that dowsers are most successful in their efforts to locate groundwater when they use tools that are typically employed by geologists and hydrologists.
The results do not help to refute skeptics' arguments, because the results provide evidence for dowsing's efficacy in only one type of terrain.

questions.prompt: The passage provides information most helpful in answering which one of the following questions?

Is the success of dowsers affected by rainstorms that may have saturated the ground in the area being dowsed?
What proportion of successful dowsers use forked sticks in locating groundwater?
