questions.prompt: The passage provides the most support for inferring which one of the following statements?

explanationBlocks.heading: Support / Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: Nothing we can do with such an open-ended question stem, other than remind ourselves to be wary of strongly worded answers or unknown comparisons on a first pass.

choices.text: Narrow, tilted fracture zones in underlying bedrock are more likely to be found in arid regions than in other regions.
choices.tag: Unknown Comparison / Out of Scope: "other regions"
choices.explanation:
This is a classic trap answer in which they take something that was said "Sarah is a cheerleader. She drives a Prius." and then they create an unsupportable answer by turning it into a comparison, "Cheerleaders are more likely to drive Prius's than other types of athletes".

We happened to hear that there were narrow, tilted fracture zones in these arid countries, but there's no comparative wording or way to know how prevalent such fracture zones are in non-arid regions.

choices.text: There are no reliable studies indicating that dowsers are consistently able to locate subsurface resources other than groundwater.
choices.tag: Too Strong: no reliable studies / Out of Scope: "other subsurface resources"
choices.explanation: This is a trap answer pattern, "The only one mentioned = the only one". The author only mentioned a reliable study about groundwater, but that doesn't imply that "there are only reliable studies about groundwater".

choices.text: A dowser attempting to locate a dry fracture zone would not use the same tools as a dowser attempting to locate groundwater.
choices.explanation:
The "dry fracture zone" part appears only in the final sentence of the passage. All we were told is that "upon request, they located a dry fracture zone". We don't have any wording that suggests they switched tools.

Given that their tools senses the presence / absence of groundwater, they could seemingly locate a dry zone by using the same tool and looking for the *absence* of whatever they feel when they sense groundwater.

choices.text: Geologists and hydrologists participating in the groundwater-locating study described in the final paragraph could not locate a dry fracture zone upon request.
choices.explanation: All we were told was that the dowsers were able to locate a dry fracture zone. Just because the passage only mentions them finding a dry zone doesn't mean that "only the dowsers found a dry zone".

choices.text: The groundwater-locating study described in the final paragraph was not a typical dowsing study.
choices.explanation:
Did we ever hear about "typical" dowsing studies?

Yes! In the middle of the 3rd paragraph we learn that "verifiably successful dowsers are not well represented in the typical study".

So, for the study in the final paragraph, were we told that "verifiably successful dowsers *are* well represented?"

Yes! In that study, they utilized "teams of the most successful dowsers".

passages.title: Trial and Appelate Court Research
passages.text:
**Passage A**

Why do some trial court judges oppose conducting independent research to help them make decisions? One of their objections is that it distorts the adversarial system by requiring an active judicial role and undermining the importance of evidence presented by the opposing parties. Another fear is that judges lack the wherewithal to conduct first-rate research and may wind up using outlier or discredited scientific materials.

While these concerns have some merit, they do not justify an absolute prohibition of the practice. First, there are reasons to sacrifice adversarial values in the scientific evidence context. The adversarial system is particularly ill-suited to handling specialized knowledge. The two parties prescreen and compensate expert witnesses, which virtually ensures conflicting and partisan testimony. At the same time, scientific facts are general truths not confined to the immediate cases. Because scientific admissibility decisions can exert considerable influence over future cases, erroneous decisions detract from the legitimacy of the system. Independent research could help judges avoid such errors.

Second, a trial provides a structure that guides any potential independent research, reducing the possibility of a judge’s reaching outlandish results. Independent research supplements, rather than replaces, the parties’ presentation of the evidence, so the parties always frame the debate.

**Passage B**

Regardless of what trial courts may do, appellate courts should resist the temptation to conduct their own independent research of scientific literature.

As a general rule, appellate courts do not hear live testimony. Thus these courts lack some of the critical tools available at the trial level for arriving at a determination of the facts: live testimony and cross- examination. Experts practicing in the field may have knowledge and experience beyond what is reflected in the available scientific literature. And adverse parties can test the credibility and reliability of proffered literature by subjecting the expert witness to the greatest legal engine ever invented for the discovery of truth—cross-examination. The trial judge may even participate in the process by questioning live witnesses. However, these events can only occur at the trial level.

Literature considered for the first time at the appellate level is not subject to live comment by practicing experts and cannot be tested in the crucible of the adversarial system. Thus one of the core criticisms against the use of such sources by appellate courts is that doing so usurps the trial court’s fact- finding function. Internet sources, in particular, have come under criticism for their potential unreliability.

When an appellate court goes outside the record to determine case facts, it ignores its function as a court of review, and it substitutes its own questionable research results for evidence that should have been tested in the trial court. This criticism applies with full force to the use of outside-the-record texts and treatises, regardless of the medium in which they are found.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Should judges and courts conduct their own independent scientific research when making decisions?

**Framework**

Present Debate

**Main Point**

The two passages debate whether it’s appropriate for judges (especially trial vs. appellate) to do independent research on scientific matters in cases: Passage A argues that trial judges should sometimes do it, while Passage B strongly urges that appellate courts should not. — Most Valuable Sentence(s): **Passage A**: "While these concerns have some merit, they do not justify an absolute prohibition of the practice." (P2) **Passage B**: "Regardless of what trial courts may do, appellate courts should resist the temptation to conduct their own independent research of scientific literature." (P1)

**Passage A: P1 – Concerns About Judges Doing Independent Research**

Some trial judges oppose doing their own scientific research because they think it undermines the adversarial system (where each side brings evidence) and because judges might not be very good at research, possibly relying on bad sources.

**Passage A: P2 – Why Some Independent Research Is Justified**

The author admits there are valid concerns, but says judges shouldn't be completely barred from doing research—especially because the adversarial system doesn't handle complex scientific evidence well and because independent research could lead to better, more accurate decisions.

**Passage A: P3 – How Independent Research Can Be Kept in Check**

A trial still keeps things under control: research adds to, but doesn't replace, the parties’ evidence, so the debate remains framed by the parties and isn’t totally freeform.

**Passage B: P1 – Appellate Courts Should Not Do Independent Research**

The author immediately takes a strong position: appellate courts shouldn’t conduct their own research into scientific literature.

**Passage B: P2 – Why Appellate Courts Are Less Suited for Fact-Finding**

Appellate courts don’t have live testimony or cross-examination—the best ways to test facts and expert opinions, which only happen at the trial level. This means they don't have the right tools to fairly evaluate complex evidence.

**Passage B: P3 – Core Criticism of Using New Research at the Appellate Level**

If appellate courts use research not discussed at trial, they go beyond their reviewing role and undermine the trial court’s job to find facts—a job best done through live comment and the adversarial process.

**Passage B: P4 – Final Critique: Appellate Courts Must Stick to the Record**

Appellate courts must avoid using information (including internet sources) that wasn’t vetted through the trial process; doing so means substituting their questionable research for proper evidence.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following principles underlies the arguments in both passages?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The two passages had pretty divergent main points, so finding a common principle will probably mean that LSAC wants us to think of something that was considered by both authors.

Psg A's author is concluding "outside research = potentially fine". Why?

- the adversarial system isn't good when it comes to specialized knowledge like science / science facts are general truths, not opposing perspectives

- judges need to get the science right, because their decisions will impact future cases

- the trial structure provides constraints that prevent judges' outside research from leading them into Crazy Town.

Psg B's author is concluding "outside research = not cool for appellate". Why?

- appellate judges don't have their outside research constrained by cross-examination and live testimony.

- doing outside research betrays what is supposed to be an appellate court's function of **reviewing**, not fact-finding.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Look for something we can apply to both passages, possibly doing with the overlapping idea of having outside research be constrained by cross-examination / live expert testimony.

choices.text: It is more appropriate for trial judges to conduct independent research than for appellate judges to do so.
choices.explanation:
Passage A doesn't take any position on appellate judges doing outside research, and Passage B doesn't take any position on trial judges doing so (she just seems tolerant of the possibility that trail judges would do outside research whereas she is not tolerant of appellate judges doing any).

Even if we to say that the author of Passage B would agree with this statement, it would be hard to argue that this plays any important role in B's overall argument.

choices.text: Judges should conduct independent research in order to determine what evidence parties to a trial should be allowed to present.
choices.explanation: This sounds pretty strong even for Passage A, but we can most easily eliminate this since it sounds like the opposite of Passage B's main point.

choices.text: Independent research by judges should not supersede evidence presented by the opposing parties in a trial.
choices.explanation:
This does work as something both authors used within their arguments.

Passage A was saying in its final paragraph that we shouldn't be so worried about trial judges doing outside research, since "a trial provides a structure that guides any potential independent research .... Independent research **supplements, rather than replaces**".

Passage B was arguing that we shouldn't let appellate judges do their own research, since it would be "ignoring its function as **a court of review**, and it substitutes its own questionable research results".

In other words, Passage A was saying, "Relax ... it's okay if trial judges to outside research. It won't supersede the adversarial testimony of the trial. The adversarial parties *always frame the debate*."

Passage B was saying, "Appellate judges shouldn't do outside research: they're just supposed to be reviewing the trial court's ruling. It would be bad for their outside research to supersede the trial court's evidence, since the appellate judge's research *is not subject to live comment by practicing experts and cannot be tested in the crucible of the adversarial system* of opposing parties."

choices.text: Judges' questioning of witnesses should be informed by the judges' own independent research.
choices.explanation: This sounds like the opposite of Passage B's main point, which is that appellate judges should **not** be doing any independent research.

choices.text: Both trial and appellate judges should conduct research based on standard, reliable sources.
choices.explanation: Passage A doesn't take any position on appellate judges and Passage B takes the position that appellate judges **should not** conduct research.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred that each author would agree that if judges conduct independent research, that research

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Working purely from passage A, under what circumstances does this author think judges could / should be doing independent research?

She thinks it makes sense to do when you're dealing with the specialized knowledge of expert witnesses giving scientific testimony. These witnesses will almost always contradict each other, and the judge needs to figure out who's right because her decision can effect scientific admissibility decisions in future cases.

She also says that if judges do research, a trial provides a good way of making sure the judge's research doesn't go too far afield of how the two lawyers have presented the evidence.

So in passage B, can we find an overlap match for
- independent research might make sense in a science trial / get it right so that future cases aren't screwed up by your crappy precedent
or
- the trial provides a structure that keeps judges's research from going too far off the grid?

B seems to disagree with the first point. He stresses that judges would be underqualified to judge the scientific stuff on their own.

But B seems to agree with the second point. He thinks that appellate judges shouldn't be doing independent research, because appellate judges aren't constrained by the adversarial structure of trial courts.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Let's look for something like,
"If judges are going to do independent research, it should be at the trial level, where the adversarial system and ability to get testimony from experts in the field will rein in the potential dangers of judges doing their own research".

choices.text: should be constrained by the structure of a trial
choices.explanation:
This is what we predicted.

It's supported by the final paragraph of passage A, and it's supported by the second paragraph of passage B.

Both author stress that the adversarial trial system is a good safeguard against judges going too far off the map with their own independent research.

choices.text: is typically confined to standard, reliable sources
choices.explanation:
The author of passage B does not take it as a typical given that judges doing their own research will confine themselves to reputable sources.

At the end of his 3rd paragraph, he seems specifically worried that judges will end up using internet sources that are unreliable.

choices.text: replaces, rather than supplements, party-presented evidence
choices.explanation: Passage A says in its final sentence that this research *supplements, rather than replaces* the evidence presented by the two parties in the trial.

choices.text: should be conducted at the trial level but not at the appellate level
choices.explanation:
There's nothing in Passage A about the appellate level, so we have no idea what A would say about that.

And Passage B did not say anything strong enough to justify that it *should* be conducted at the trial level.

choices.text: usurps the trial court's fact-finding function
choices.explanation:
A's final sentence is that independent research "supplements, rather than replaces" the evidence presented by the two lawyers. It's too strong to say that Passage A thinks that independent research ****usurps**** (overthrows) the trial court's fact-finding function.

This language comes from Passage B, which was talking about what happens when an *appellate* judge does independent research.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following phrases is used by the author of passage B to express a concern that is most closely related to the concern expressed by the author of passage A using the phrase "lack the wherewithal" (final sentence of the first paragraph of passage A)?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
When Passage A says that "judges lack the wherewithal to conduct first-rate research and may wind up using outlier or discredited scientific materials", it's saying something like they lack the ****ability / savvy**** to distinguish good info from sketchy stuff.

So let's pick whatever answer is a moment from passage B where we're questioning whether judges have enough savvy / expertise to know how to get solid research info on their own.

choices.text: experience beyond what is reflected
choices.explanation: This phrase is used about experts, not about the judges doing potentially un-savvy research.

choices.text: may even participate in the process
choices.explanation: This comes from a line talking about a judge during a trial, talking to a live witness. So it has nothing to do with a judge, on her own time, doing research.

choices.text: subject to live comment
choices.explanation:
This is not about judges doing their own sketchy research. It's saying that once they've done their research, any new evidence they would find and then enter into the record for an appellate ruling would not be subjected to cross examination scrutiny.

This is the potential danger of judges doing their own sketchy research, but it's not directly talking about the research, the way the correct answer is.

choices.text: questionable research results
choices.explanation: This is the best match for judges doing their own sketchy research, lacking the wherewithal to tell the difference between reputable info and more questionable info.

choices.text: outside-the-record texts
choices.explanation: This phrase is talking about the materials the judges would be reading while doing their independent research, but nothing in this phrase captures the idea of "sketchy / un-savvy / flawed" the way that *lack of wherewithal / questionable research results* does.

questions.prompt: Given the statements about cross-examination in the fourth sentence of the second paragraph of passage B, the author of passage B would be most likely to take issue with which one of the following claims by the author of passage A?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
*Cross-examination* definitely showed up in Passage B. In the 2nd paragraph, the author refers to cross-examination as "one of the critical tools available at the trial level for arriving at a determination of the facts".

Later in that paragraph she says, "adverse parties can test the credibility and reliability of proffered literature by subjecting the expert witness to the greatest legal engine ever invested for the discovery of truth: cross-examination".

So Passage B is a big fan of cross-examination and greatly respects its capacity to determine facts.

Passage A never directly mentions cross-examination, but it mentions "the adversarial system" which is related. The adversarial system of justice refers to the idea of two lawyers, one fighting for a guilty verdict, one fighting for an acquittal. They each can present their own evidence and witnesses, and they can each cross-examine the other lawyer's witnesses.

Passage A says in its 2nd paragraph, "The adversarial system is particularly ill-suited to handling specialized knowledge. The two parties prescreen and compensate expert witnesses, which virtually ensures conflicting and partisan testimony".

In other words, Passage A thinks it's okay for judges to do some of their own research because judges are not able to ascertain the scientific facts by listening to the two lawyers present adversarial testimony from expert witnesses.

Meanwhile, Passage B thinks it's bad for appellate judges to so their own research, because he thinks that cross-examination (which appellate judges don't get to hear) is crucial when it comes to ascertaining the scientific facts.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Passage B would probably say to Passage A, "What do you mean that the adversarial system is particularly ill-suited to handing expert testimony?! That's crazy. Don't you know that adverse parties can test the credibility and reliability of the expert witnesses by subjecting them to cross-examination?"

choices.text: An absolute prohibition of independent research by trial judges is not justified.
choices.explanation: This sentence has nothing to do with cross-examination. Also Passage B wouldn't necessarily disagree with this. She never takes a stand on whether judges at the trial court level should be allowed to do independent research.

choices.text: The adversarial system is particularly ill-suited to handling specialized knowledge.
choices.explanation: This is what we anticipated. Passage B would disagree with this, because passage B thinks that the adversarial system involves cross-examination, which allows "adverse parties to test the credibility and reliability of the expert witnesses".

choices.text: Scientific admissibility decisions exert considerable influence over future cases.
choices.explanation:
This sentence has nothing to do with cross-examination.

Also Passage B wouldn't necessarily disagree with this. She never takes a stand on whether scientific admissibility decisions influence future cases (presumably both authors believe in the idea that future cases rely on precedent).

choices.text: Erroneous decisions can be readily exposed by third parties.
choices.explanation:
Passage A never really says that erroneous decisions can be easily exposed by a third party.

He says that "erroneous decision detract from the legitimacy of the system". And he thinks that a trial provides a structure that guides independent research, reducing the possibility of a judge's reaching outlandish results .

Passage B would probably agree with all these things, and none of this really has anything to do with Passage B's thoughts on cross-examination.

choices.text: A trial provides a structure that guides any potential independent research.
choices.explanation:
Because of Passage B's firm confidence in cross-examination, she would potentially agree that an adversarial trial constrains the judge's fact-finding.

Passage B doesn't want independent research at the appellate level because judges at the appellate level *don't* have a structure constraining their potential independent research.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following words as used in passage B comes closest to having the same reference as the word "crucible" in the first sentence of the third paragraph of passage B?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The word 'crucible' means something "high-pressure, strained, arduous, difficult".

For most of us non-popular kids, getting through the *crucible* of high school was a daily struggle.

For LSAT students, confident as we may be in our untimed practice, when we subject ourselves to the *crucible* of a timed test, we see more careless mistakes occur.

So we want an answer that sounds like "difficult, strained, arduous task".

choices.text: temptation
choices.explanation: The temptation to conduct your own investigation could result in a "difficult, strained, arduous task" of finding the information online, but the ****difficult task**** would match the noun "investigation", not "temptation".

choices.text: credibility
choices.explanation:
*Credibility* means the trustworthiness or believability of someone or something.

That doesn't match up well with "difficult, strained, arduous task".

choices.text: engine
choices.explanation:
Certainly the word "engine" by itself would not mean "difficult, strained, arduous task", but in the context of this sentence this works.

The verb we're using is *subjected to*. That verb almost always is followed by [something terrible].

*My roommate was subjected to my early days of learning the violin.*

*She was subjected to three days of torture before she gave the interrogators the information they were looking for.*

*He was subjected to harsh cross-examination by the prosecutor.*

Being cross-examined is definitely a high-pressure, strained, arduous task for most people. When you're done and can leave the stand, most people will breathe a huge sigh of relief that "THAT crucible is finally over".

It also helps that *crucible* is used in reference to the ****adversarial**** system, which refers to a trial in which one lawyer (the prosecutor) is "fighting" her adversary, the other lawyer (the defense lawyer). The sentence with "engine" begins by saying, "****adverse**** parties can subject an expert" ... to the crucible of the adversarial system.

choices.text: function
choices.explanation:
"function" is being used in a way that means the trial court's "job / responsibility / domain".

Fact-finding could be a "difficult, strained, high-pressure, arduous task", but it's not being presented that way in this sentence. It just sounds more like, "Hey that was Louie's job / function, not yours".

choices.text: medium
choices.explanation:
The word "medium" is being used to mean "the format / the source" in which something is found.

This has nothing to do with a high-pressure experience with adversity, i.e. a crucible.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred, based on their titles, that the relationship between which one of the following pairs of documents is most analogous to the relationship between passage A and passage B, respectively?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
We need to articulate the relationship between the two passages in a generic way, so that we can match that up with titles about other topics.

We know that Passage A was saying, "Independent research is okay in some cases, and for these reasons".

And Passage B was saying, "Appellate courts should not do independent research."

So the big relationship is that the two authors are expressing different feelings about a very similar topic:

A: We shouldn't totally prohibit X. There are reasons to be okay with X sometimes.

B: We should totally prohibit X.

But the two authors weren't explicitly disagreeing, because A is talking about trial judges and B is talking about appellate judges.

So let's look for something like
"X is okay sometimes, in *this* context"
vs.
"X is not okay, in *this other* context"

choices.text: "Negative Effects of Salt Consumption" "Unhealthy Amounts of Salt in the Diet"
choices.explanation:
We were hoping that Passage A's would sound more positive, like the author is *defending* the potential value of something that other people are trashing.

In this answer, both answers seem to be stressing negatives about salt.

choices.text: "Salt Can Be Beneficial for Some People" "People with High Blood Pressure Should Avoid Salt"
choices.explanation:
This is our best match for
"X is okay in some cases"
"X is not cool, in this other context"

Passage A is saying "independent research by judges can sometimes be beneficial".

Passage B is saying "judges on appellate courts should avoid independent research".

choices.text: "Debunking the Alleged Danger Posed by Salt" "Inconclusive Research Results on the Health Effects of Salt Consumption"
choices.explanation:
The first title is a pretty usable one for Passage A, who is responding to people who think that independent research by judges is a scary thing we should avoid. She argues that we don't have to totally avoid independent research, and in doing so she is debunking some of the opponents' fears.

But the title for B has no sense of "we should not do X". It says that there are *inconclusive* research results, which would leave us without any takeaway. Meanwhile, passage B had a very strong and clear takeaway.

choices.text: "Substitutes for Dietary Salt" "Salt Substitutes Come Under Fire"
choices.explanation:
The 2nd title here would make some sense for Passage A, since Passage A is responding to people who oppose independent research.

It's still not a great match, because it sounds like it's just describing that controversy, rather conveying the author's opinion. A better title for passage A would be, "Salt Substitutes Come Under *Excessive* Fire".

But this answer isn't even offering that for Passage A. Passage B doesn't have anything in it that sounds like it's describing some thing that has become the target of popular criticism.

The most charitable read of this answer would be thinking of "Substitutes" as "Independent Research" (and Dietary Salt would be the research presented at the trial).

We'd get titles like
"Judges' Substituting for Research Presented at Trial"
and
"Independent Research Comes Under Fire"

We'd still say that the title for A conveys too little of the author's main point, and we'd say that the title for B suggests that passage B discusses a recent controversy, whereas it does not. Passage B just offers the author's opinion. It never places this in a broader "fight" that's going on.

choices.text: "The Health Effects of Salt Consumption" "Salt Deficiency in a Sample Population"
choices.explanation:
The first title is totally neutral. It isn't saying that Salt Consumption has healthy effects. We could title something, "The Health Effects of Taking Meth" and we wouldn't anticipate hearing good things about meth.

Meanwhile, passage A was not neutral.

The second title is also neutral. It seems to just be a descriptive article about a population that didn't get enough salt.

These titles are supposed to capture the essential relationship between the two passages, and that relationship was that Passage A was defending independent research while Passage B was critiquing independent research.

questions.prompt: The stances of the authors of passage A and passage B, respectively, toward independent research on the part of trial judges are most accurately described as

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
What line references do we have for "independent research by trial judges" in passage A and B?

Passage B memorably *starts* with a little aside about trial courts, before going on to talk about appellate courts for the rest of the passage.

The first line of B says, "Regardless of what trial courts may do, appellate courts should not allow independent research by judges".

So the author of B has ****no**** stance when it comes to trial judges ... "*regardless* of what they do" is not taking any position on them.

Passage A's author's main point is found in the first sentence of its 2nd paragraph:
*The concerns about independent research by trial judges does not justify an absolute prohibition*.

Okay, if someone thinks "X should not be absolutely prohibited", what's an easier way to say that?

*X should sometimes be allowed*?

So what kind of stance do you have if you're saying, "I think we should sometimes allow judges to do their own research"?

You have a somewhat positive, sympathetic, accommodating stance.

The author of passage B? He had a neutral, noncommittal stance.

choices.text: resigned acceptance and implicit disapproval
choices.tag: Bad Match for A and B
choices.explanation:
*Resigned* acceptance means, "sigh, fine. I'll accept it, I guess."

The author of A wasn't being forced by anyone to tolerate independent research by judges. She was writing this essay, sticking up for its validity. That's more positive and proactive than "resigned acceptance".

Passage B is explicitly noncommittal to the subject of trial judges, so we're not allowed to infer any attitude from passage B, even *implicit* negativity.

choices.text: cautious ambivalence and strict neutrality
choices.explanation:
Passage B was certainly neutral, so that part's good.

But we want a more positive description for A: amenable, sympathetic, agreeable

This author is writing this passage in response to people who want to totally prohibit independent research by judges. She is defending the practice, saying it has merits and there are safeguards against its potential drawbacks.

*Cautious Ambivalence* is like, "Ohhhh, boy. I'm not sure about this. I dont know if I'm gonna like this."

To be ambivalent (ambi + valence = both charges) is to have both positive and negative feelings in a way that cancels out. You feel unsettled by indecision, because you don't know whether you like it or not.

choices.text: reasoned skepticism and veiled antipathy
choices.tag: Bad Match for A and B
choices.explanation:
We want something positive for passage A, and reasoned skepticism is not positive (it's not super negative, but it's definitely not positive).

The author of A didn't seem tepid, ambivalent, cautious, skeptical, resigned. She wrote a passage to stick up for the practice of independent research.

Passage B is explicitly noncommittal to the subject of trial judges, so we're not allowed to infer any attitude from passage B, even *veiled* negativity.

Antipathy (anti + pathos = bad feeling) means strong dislike. Whenever we run into an ex-boyfriend or girlfriend and we tell them that our new relationship is going well, that disingenuous smile on our ex's face while they're saying, "I'm so happy for you!" is *veiled antipathy*.

choices.text: qualified approval and explicit noncommitment
choices.explanation:
Passage B was definitely explicitly noncommittal, because it just quickly opened with, "Regardless of whatever trial courts do, *appellate courts* ...."

(I actually predicted the right words! Didn't expect that)

Passage A's portion is a little tougher to love, but we're happy to see that the main noun is *approval*.

*Qualified* approval means that you approve of something, but with some qualms / exceptions.

If I say, "I'm glad Biden got elected, but I don't think he'll do enough to address climate change", that's qualified approval. If I say, "The movie was pretty good. I liked all the parts with the car chases", that's qualified approval.

The author's main point sentence (the first sentence of the 2nd paragraph), expresses qualified approval.

*Qualm / qualification*:
while these concerns have some merit

*Approval*
Some cases of this practice should be tolerated
(this practice should not be 100% prohibited)

choices.text: forceful advocacy and tentative opposition
choices.tag: Bad Match for A and B
choices.explanation:
The easiest way to eliminate is the passage B option. Only two of the five answers showed that passage B had a neutral / noncommittal stance. This answer says that B was "opposing".

Additionally, the descriptor *****forceful***** *advocacy* is too strong for passage (A), who says "the concerns about independent research by judges do have some merit".
